claims.text: Spark plasma sintering of refractory high-entropy alloy elements with copper enables rapid, large-scale reaction and densification.
Rapid SPS processing suppresses diffusion-driven segregation associated with the positive heat of mixing between refractory elements and copper.
SPS yields a stable and uniform RHEA-Cu composite microstructure.
Rapid heating and controlled pressure during SPS can minimize the time available for diffusion.
Minimizing diffusion time reduces the tendency of refractory elements and copper to segregate.
SPS produces a refined, ultrafine-grained microstructure in the RHEA-Cu composite.
SPS produces a homogeneous phase distribution at RHEA-Cu interfaces.
The short SPS cycle limits diffusion processes that would otherwise exacerbate segregation associated with positive heat of mixing.
Applied pressure during SPS promotes densification and strong bonding in the composite.
The SPS-processed composite will have greater microstructural stability than a conventionally sintered composite.
The SPS-processed composite will have better mechanical properties than a conventionally sintered composite.
Conventional sintering uses longer heating periods than SPS.
Longer conventional-sintering periods increase phase segregation and microstructural instability in RHEA-Cu composites.
Uneven temperature distribution during scale-up can reduce the effectiveness of SPS.
Failure to control SPS temperature, time, and pressure optimally can reduce process effectiveness.
Long-term reactor irradiation may create additional challenges for the proposed RHEA-Cu composite.
